hawaii.damages_note: Fair and just compensation for pecuniary injury and loss of love and affection, including loss of society, companionship, comfort, consortium or protection; loss of marital, filial or parental care, training, guidance or education; and lost financial support. The estate may recover reasonable expenses of the last illness and burial. The statute provides only compensatory damages; it does not provide for punitive damages.
hawaii.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death. If the defendant concealed responsibility, the clock starts when the concealment is discovered (or should have been), with up to 6 years to file (HRS § 657-20). A person under 18 at the time of death has 2 years from turning 18 (HRS § 657-13).
hawaii.state_note: Reciprocal beneficiaries (Hawaii's registered-partner status) are expressly included as eligible claimants, and damages other than last-illness and burial expenses do not become part of the deceased person's estate.
hawaii.who_can_file: The deceased person's legal representative (personal representative of the estate) may file, or the surviving spouse, reciprocal beneficiary, children, parents, or any person wholly or partly dependent on the deceased may file for their own losses (Haw. Rev. Stat. § 663-3).

idaho.damages_note: Such damages as are just under the circumstances, including lost earnings and support, funeral and burial expenses, medical expenses, and loss of companionship and society. Noneconomic damages are capped at about $538,000 per claimant (Idaho Code § 6-1603, as adjusted effective July 1, 2026); economic losses are not capped.
idaho.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (Idaho Code § 5-219(4)). If a government entity is involved, a tort-claim notice must be filed within 180 days (Idaho Code § 6-906).
idaho.state_note: Idaho defines 'heirs' more broadly than most states: stepchildren qualify without proving dependency, and dependent blood relatives, adoptive siblings and a dependent putative spouse can also qualify. The claim belongs to the heirs, not to the estate.
idaho.who_can_file: The deceased person's heirs, or the personal representative of the estate on the heirs' behalf, may file (Idaho Code § 5-311). 'Heirs' includes the spouse, children, stepchildren and parents, plus dependent blood relatives and adoptive siblings, and a dependent putative spouse.

illinois.damages_note: Fair and just compensation for pecuniary injuries, including funeral and burial expenses, lost financial support and earnings, loss of consortium and companionship, loss of instruction and moral training for children, and grief, sorrow and mental suffering. Punitive damages are available when applicable, except in healing-art or legal-malpractice cases and against the State or a unit of local government. There is generally no cap, except for claims against the State in the Court of Claims.
illinois.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death. A claim based on violent intentional conduct may be filed within 5 years of death, or within 1 year after the final disposition of the criminal case. A beneficiary who was under 18 has 2 years after turning 18.
illinois.state_note: Prairie State serves northern and central Illinois outside Cook County; if there is no surviving spouse or next of kin entitled to recover, damages are limited to hospital, medical, funeral and estate-administration costs.
illinois.who_can_file: Only the personal representative of the deceased person's estate may file, for the exclusive benefit of the surviving spouse and next of kin (740 ILCS 180/2). If the estate has no personal representative, the court can appoint a special administrator.

indiana.damages_note: Under the general statute (decedent left a spouse, dependent children or dependent next of kin): reasonable medical, hospital, funeral and burial expenses, lost earnings, value of household services, and loss of love, care, affection, society and companionship, with no general cap. Under the adult statute (unmarried adult with no dependents, Ind. Code § 34-23-1-2): medical, funeral and burial expenses, estate administration costs, and loss of love and companionship capped at $300,000 in total; lost earnings are not recoverable. Under the child statute (Ind. Code § 34-23-2-1): loss of the child's services, love and companionship, and related counseling costs.
indiana.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death, for both adult and child decedents. The period is a condition of the right to sue rather than an ordinary limitations period, so the usual extensions generally do not apply; fraudulent concealment by the defendant is the main recognized exception. Separate, shorter tort-claim notice deadlines apply against government entities.
indiana.state_note: Indiana has three separate wrongful-death statutes, and which one applies — general, adult, or child — depends on the decedent's age and whether they left a spouse or dependents; the choice sharply changes what can be recovered.
indiana.who_can_file: For an adult, only the personal representative of the estate may file (Ind. Code § 34-23-1-1). For a child (under 20, or under 23 if enrolled in school, or a viable fetus), a parent or legal guardian may file directly (Ind. Code § 34-23-2-1).

iowa.damages_note: Medical and hospital expenses for the last illness or injury, funeral and burial expenses (with interest from the date of death), lost wages and benefits, the value of the deceased spouse's, parent's or child's services and support, and the deceased person's pain and suffering before death. There is no statutory cap on wrongful-death damages. Damages generally pass as property of the estate, except damages for loss of services and support, which the court apportions among the surviving spouse, children and parents.
iowa.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (Iowa Code § 614.1(2)). Against the State, a written claim must be filed within 2 years and suit within 6 months after the claim is decided or denied (Iowa Code § 669.13).
iowa.state_note: Iowa has no single named Wrongful Death Act: the claim survives to the estate under the survival statutes, and section 633.336 controls how damages are divided. Wrongful-death damages are generally not subject to the estate's debts when the decedent leaves a spouse, child or parent.
iowa.who_can_file: The personal representative of the estate must file the claim (Iowa Code §§ 611.20, 611.22). If a minor child has died, the parents or legal guardians may file directly (Iowa Code § 613.15A).

kansas.damages_note: Pecuniary (financial) losses, such as lost earnings and support, medical and care expenses, and funeral expenses, are not capped. Nonpecuniary losses — mental anguish, suffering or bereavement; loss of society, companionship, comfort or protection; loss of marital, filial or parental care, training, guidance or education — are capped at $250,000 in total (K.S.A. § 60-1903). Funeral expenses and care expenses are not counted toward that cap (K.S.A. § 60-1904).
kansas.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (K.S.A. § 60-513(a)(5)).
kansas.state_note: Kansas is unusual in letting any heir who suffered a loss start the case, rather than requiring the estate's personal representative to file.
kansas.who_can_file: Any heir at law of the deceased who suffered a loss because of the death may file (K.S.A. § 60-1902) — typically the surviving spouse, children, parents, grandparents or siblings. Other heirs who suffered a loss may join or intervene, and the recovery benefits all heirs who suffered a loss whether or not they joined.

kentucky.damages_note: Damages focus on the deceased person's lost earning power, plus funeral expenses, medical expenses, and administration and recovery costs. The deceased person's pain and suffering before death can be recovered through a survival claim joined with the wrongful-death claim. Punitive damages may be recovered if the act was willful or the negligence was gross. There is no statutory cap. A surviving spouse may separately claim loss of consortium (KRS § 411.145), and parents of a minor child may claim loss of the child's affection and companionship (KRS § 411.135).
kentucky.deadline_note: Generally 1 year from the date of death (KRS § 413.140). The personal representative gets 1 year from the date of appointment to file (KRS § 413.180), but the outside limit is ordinarily 2 years from the date of death.
kentucky.state_note: The statute fixes the order in which the recovery is divided: all to the spouse if there are no children; half to the spouse and half to the children if there are children; all to the children if there is no spouse; then to the parents if there is no spouse or child. Kentucky's wrongful-death right comes from the state constitution (Ky. Const. § 241). Note: Kentucky Legal Aid serves south-central and western Kentucky only; other regions have separate legal-aid programs.
kentucky.who_can_file: Only the personal representative of the deceased person's estate may file; individual family members cannot file on their own (Ky. Rev. Stat. § 411.130). If no estate has been opened, one must be opened and a personal representative appointed first.

louisiana.damages_note: Loss of love, affection and companionship, grief and mental anguish, loss of financial support and household services, and funeral and burial expenses. There is no general cap, but the statutory medical-malpractice damages limit applies to wrongful-death claims against health-care providers. Medical expenses and the deceased person's pain and suffering between injury and death are recovered through a separate survival action (La. Civ. Code art. 2315.1).
louisiana.deadline_note: The longer of 1 year from the date of death or 2 years from the date the injury or damage was sustained. For medical-malpractice deaths, the period is 1 year from the date of death.
louisiana.state_note: Louisiana is a civil-law state, so the claim comes from the Civil Code rather than a common-law wrongful-death act, and it creates two separate claims from one death: the family's wrongful-death claim and the deceased person's survival claim. Southeast Louisiana Legal Services serves 22 parishes in southeast Louisiana only; other regions have separate legal-aid programs.
louisiana.who_can_file: Surviving family members file in a strict priority order, and only the highest surviving class may sue: (1) surviving spouse and children; (2) if none, surviving parents; (3) if none, surviving siblings; (4) if none, surviving grandparents (La. Civ. Code art. 2315.2). A parent who abandoned the deceased during minority is treated as not surviving.

maine.damages_note: Fair and just compensation for pecuniary injuries, including medical, surgical and hospital expenses, funeral expenses, and lost earnings and support — pecuniary damages are not capped. Loss of comfort, society and companionship, including emotional distress, is capped at $1,000,000, adjusted for inflation for deaths after 2023. Punitive damages are capped at $500,000.
maine.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death. If the death was caused by a homicide, the action may be filed within 6 years after the personal representative or special administrator discovers there is a just cause of action against the person who caused the homicide.
maine.state_note: The recovery goes directly to the heirs in the proportions set by Maine's intestacy laws and does not become part of the probate estate, except for amounts specifically awarded to the estate for medical and funeral expenses — so it is generally not available to the estate's creditors.
maine.who_can_file: Only the personal representative or special administrator of the deceased person's estate may file; a spouse, child or parent cannot file individually (18-C M.R.S. § 2-807). The court can appoint a special administrator to pursue the claim.

maryland.damages_note: Damages proportioned to each beneficiary's injury, including lost earnings and support, funeral expenses, mental anguish and emotional pain and suffering, and loss of society, companionship, comfort, protection, and marital, parental or filial care, training, guidance or education. Economic damages are not capped. Noneconomic damages are capped at $965,000 for a single beneficiary for claims arising October 1, 2025–September 30, 2026, rising by $15,000 each October 1; with multiple beneficiaries the cap is 150% of the single-beneficiary cap (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-108). Punitive damages are not available under the wrongful-death statute.
maryland.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death. If an occupational disease caused the death, the deadline is within 10 years of death or within 3 years of discovering the cause of death, whichever is shorter. The period is tolled while a beneficiary is a minor or mentally incompetent (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 5-201).
maryland.state_note: Maryland is unusual in giving families 3 years to file, and its noneconomic-damages cap rises by $15,000 every October 1, so the cap that applies depends on when the claim arose.
maryland.who_can_file: The deceased person's spouse, parents and children (primary beneficiaries) may file; if none survive, any person related by blood or marriage who was substantially dependent on the deceased may file (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-904). Only one wrongful-death action may be filed for a death.
